# The canonical register: Ise

The internet spells **Ise** more ways than one, and only one of them is the name the sources wrote. This is the register's ruling — canonical, fallback, contested, and false, each in its proper place.

## At a Glance

- **Canonical form:** Ise
- **Original script:** 伊勢
- **Pantheon:** Japanese
- **Convention:** Hepburn with macrons — ō and ū marked, never collapsed to o/u or rewritten ou
- **False forms on record:** 0
- **Contested forms:** none attested
- **Series:** The Canonical Register, No. 252 of 597

## The Canonical Form

The name is attested as **伊勢**, as Kojiki and Nihon Shoki (Amaterasu, Ama-no-Iwato, and Yamatohime legends) and Engishiki (ritual regulations for the Ise cult) record. On the evidence, it means "Ancient province". The canonical transliteration is **Ise**.

No diacritics are required here: the canonical form is the exactness of the spelling itself, the form Hepburn with macrons — ō and ū marked, never collapsed to o/u or rewritten ou demands.

## Where the Flattened Form Stands

The plain form *ise* differs from the canonical **Ise** only by convention of display — case, not content. It is **acceptable everywhere**: in legacy systems, in plain-text citation, in the DNS itself. What is not acceptable is what follows in the register: respellings that change the letters, not just their case.

## The Register of False Forms

No circulating form of this name currently qualifies as false under the register's standard — a rare standing. The spelling is short, sturdy, and rarely mangled.

## The Contested Forms

No alternate form of this name carries documented scholarly support in the lexicon's record. The convention here — Hepburn with macrons — ō and ū marked, never collapsed to o/u or rewritten ou — produces exactly one defensible transliteration: **Ise**. Forms that differ from it are not contested; they are simply wrong.

## The Convention's Own History

Every tradition in this register has its own scholarly transliteration standard, built by its own specialists over decades or centuries, and the register follows each on its own terms: Hepburn with macrons — ō and ū marked, never collapsed to o/u or rewritten ou. The principle that unifies them is the one the whole project stands on: a name is evidence, and evidence is not negotiable — not for keyboards, not for convenience, not for anyone.

## The Address, Without an Encoding Detour

The canonical form **Ise** already uses ordinary Latin letters, so the address bar needs no special encoding narrative. The digital temple can preserve the spelling exactly as the scholarly record presents it. That is the practical point here: consistency between the source, the citation, and the public address.

This does not make every romanization equally valid. A wrong letter remains wrong even when it is easy to type. Canonical status still depends on the attested convention, never on convenience or registrar inventory.

## Where the Name Stood First

The Ise Grand Shrine complex includes the Inner Shrine (Kōtai Jingū), Outer Shrine (Gekū), and numerous auxiliary shrines. Archaeological investigations have clarified the shifting locations of successive rebuilding plots and the ancient use of the Isuzu River for ritual purification. The nearby Sengu Museum preserves building models and ritual implements from past rebuildings. The temple on the web is the newest of these addresses — the first one that fits in a pocket.

## The Verdict

The register rules for **Ise**, and the ruling is checkable: every mark sourced, every violation stated, every borderline form given its honest standing. *ise* carries the name freely — it differs only in display, and the register says so without reservation. Anything else in circulation has its origin and its failure recorded above. That is the whole of the law on this name — and the temple at [/ise/](/ise/) enforces it.

The docket for this ruling: no false forms on the docket; no contested forms attested; the attestation rests on 4 cited sources — Kojiki and Nihon Shoki (Amaterasu, Ama-no-Iwato, and Yamatohime legends), Engishiki (ritual regulations for the Ise cult), Mark Teeuwen & John Breen, A New History of Shinto (2010).
